newsitem.title: USA: NASA looks to fix stuck panel on Mars probe.
newsitem.headline: NASA looks to fix stuck panel on Mars probe.

text.p: A U.S. space probe fired its engine on Thursday to place it on course for Mars, while engineers tried to find ways of freeing its jammed solar panel, the mission manager said.

The Mars Global Surveyor, which blasted off from Cape Canaveral on Nov. 7, placed itself on course for Mars with a 44-second firing of its engine at 11 a.m. EST (1600 GMT) on Thursday as it flew through space at 74,000 mph (119,000 kph).
"It was very important," mission manager Glenn Cunningham said. "This is the big one that actually gets us headed at the right spot. Without this burn we would have sailed past Mars."
Three further rocket firings are planned during the journey to Mars to fine tune the probe's trajectory.
As Global Surveyor headed into deep space, engineers were trying to determine how to fix one of two wing-like solar panels that failed to open properly after blastoff.
The balky panel is generating electricity as planned, but could cause problems once the spacecraft arrives at Mars next September.

The spacecraft is supposed to dip into the thin Martian atmosphere, using the backs of its solar panels as air brakes to slow down and round off its orbit. If the panel remains bent, however, it is likely to collapse under the force of the manoeuvre, Cunningham said.
Engineers suspect a two-inch (five-cm) lever arm in the solar panel deployment mechanism broke off and became lodged in a joint, jamming the wing about 20 degrees from its intended position.
Cunningham hopes a jolt from the probe's rocket engine will dislodge the broken lever, allowing the panel to swing fully open.
If it cannot be freed, the front of the panels, on which the electricity-generating solar cells are mounted, would have to be used for the so-called aerobraking manuever.
"We are examining very carefully whether we can safely do the aerobraking with the cell side into the flow," said Cunningham.
Engineers plan tests with a duplicate array on the ground to check that the solar cells will not be damaged during the braking process.
Cunningham said project officials are optimistic the panel can be freed or that an alternative aerobraking manuever can be devised.
"It looks very hopeful for us," he said. "We have a number of ways to go here and I'm not particularly concerned."
Over the weekend, Mars Global Surveyor will test its camera and other instruments on the earth and moon, which by then will be three million miles (4.8 million km) away.
"The (earth's) disc will be very small and therefore features will not be discernable," Cunningham said. "I don't think we are going to see any signs of intelligent life."
